output.executive_summary: The brief reports an observational study of 48 Riverton neighborhoods, using July afternoon satellite measurements from 2023 to 2025, and finds that greater tree canopy was associated with lower land-surface temperatures after accounting for impervious surfaces and building density [S1][S2]. Eastgate was the hottest neighborhood and Willow Park the coolest, while impervious surface was the strongest single predictor of temperature [S3]. July heat-related emergency calls were higher in the hottest neighborhood quartile than in the coolest [S3]. The authors recommend prioritizing planting in Eastgate and Millbrook and setting a citywide 30% canopy target by 2035; they estimate 6,000 street trees would cost about $2.1 million over ten years [S4]. The brief cautions that land-surface temperature is not air temperature and that its cross-sectional findings show association, not causation [S4].
output.detailed_summary:
The research brief, dated September 2026, describes a study of 48 Riverton neighborhoods between 2023 and 2025. It reports that each 10-percentage-point increase in tree canopy cover was associated with a 1.4°C decrease in average afternoon land-surface temperature, after accounting for impervious surfaces and building density. The brief presents this as support for targeted planting in the hottest neighborhoods [S1].

Canopy cover was measured using 2024 aerial imagery and ranged from 6% to 41%. The researchers derived land-surface temperature from 36 cloud-free satellite passes in July of 2023, 2024 and 2025, all between 1:00 and 3:00 p.m. They used a multiple regression model with average afternoon land-surface temperature as the outcome and canopy cover, impervious-surface share, and building density as predictors [S2].

Eastgate, with 6% canopy, had the highest average afternoon surface temperature at 41.2°C. Willow Park, with 41% canopy, had the lowest at 34.8°C, a difference of 6.4°C. Impervious-surface share was the strongest single predictor of surface temperature, followed by canopy cover. July heat-related emergency calls were 23% higher in the hottest quartile of neighborhoods than in the coolest quartile [S3].

The brief notes that land-surface temperature is not the same as the air temperature people experience, that the cross-sectional design establishes association rather than causation, and that the 2024 imagery may not reflect trees planted since then. It recommends prioritizing planting in Eastgate and Millbrook and setting a citywide canopy target of 30% by 2035. The estimated cost of planting 6,000 street trees is about $2.1 million over ten years [S4].

output.executive_summary: The brief reports a study of 48 Riverton neighborhoods using satellite measurements from July afternoons between 2023 and 2025. It finds that each 10-percentage-point increase in tree canopy cover was associated with a 1.4°C lower average afternoon land-surface temperature after accounting for impervious surfaces and building density; the brief also identifies impervious surface as the strongest single predictor [S1][S2][S3]. Eastgate was the hottest neighborhood and Willow Park the coolest, while heat-related emergency calls were higher in the hottest quartile [S3]. The authors recommend prioritizing planting in Eastgate and Millbrook, pursuing a citywide 30% canopy target by 2035, and estimate a ten-year cost of about $2.1 million for 6,000 street trees [S4]. They caution that land-surface temperature is not air temperature, the study shows association rather than causation, and the 2024 imagery may not reflect later planting [S4].
output.detailed_summary:
The September 2026 research brief by Dr. Amara Nwosu and Kenji Morita of the Riverton Institute for Urban Studies summarizes a study of 48 Riverton neighborhoods between 2023 and 2025. It reports that each 10-percentage-point increase in tree canopy cover was associated with a 1.4°C lower average afternoon surface temperature, after accounting for impervious surfaces and building density. The brief presents this as support for targeted planting in the hottest neighborhoods [S1].

For its methods, the study measured neighborhood tree canopy from 2024 aerial imagery; canopy cover ranged from 6% to 41%. Land-surface temperature (LST) was derived from 36 cloud-free satellite passes in July of 2023, 2024 and 2025, all between 1:00 and 3:00 p.m. The researchers used a multiple regression model with average afternoon LST as the outcome and canopy cover, share of impervious surface, and building density as predictors [S2].

The results identify Eastgate, with 6% canopy, as the hottest neighborhood, averaging 41.2°C, and Willow Park, with 41% canopy, as the coolest, averaging 34.8°C—a difference of 6.4°C. The brief says share of impervious surface was the strongest single predictor of surface temperature and canopy cover was the second strongest. Heat-related emergency calls during July were 23% higher in the hottest quartile of neighborhoods than in the coolest quartile [S3].

The authors note that LST is not the same as the air temperature people experience, that the cross-sectional design shows association rather than causation, and that the 2024 imagery may not reflect trees planted since then. They recommend prioritizing planting in Eastgate and Millbrook and setting a citywide target of 30% canopy cover by 2035. The brief estimates that planting 6,000 street trees would cost about $2.1 million over ten years [S4].

findings.topic: Approved budget and forecast at completion
findings.description: Both documents state an approved budget of $180,000 and a forecast at completion of $186,500, implying a $6,500 overrun [S2][S4].

The finance memo’s schedule assumes go-live on December 1, 2026. The documents provide different dates without explaining whether the schedule changed or whether the memo uses a separate planning assumption [S1][S5].

The status report lists Finance’s confirmation of $6,500 in contingency funding by October 31, 2026 as an action item. The finance memo recommends that the steering committee approve $6,500 from the technology reserve. Both address funding the same forecast overrun, but the memo presents a recommendation rather than confirmation or approval [S3][S4].

The finance memo asks the project team to confirm whether staff training costs of $7,800 are included in the forecast at completion. The status report mentions staff training as in progress and an action to circulate a revised schedule, but does not state whether training costs are included in the forecast [S2][S3][S5].
The finance memo specifies a final implementation installment of $9,000.00 payable to Larkspur in December 2026. The status report does not provide an installment amount or payment date [S2][S5].

findings.topic: Project progress and risks versus finance focus
findings.description: The status report includes migration progress (412,000 of 485,000 records, or 85%), milestones, risks, and action items; the finance memo instead focuses on budget position, a schedule assumption, and an open question about training costs. The memo does not provide an updated migration-progress or risk status [S1][S2][S3][S4][S5].

output.detailed_summary:
The research brief, dated September 2026 and authored by Dr. Amara Nwosu and Kenji Morita of the Riverton Institute for Urban Studies, reports a study of 48 Riverton neighborhoods between 2023 and 2025. It finds that each 10-percentage-point increase in tree canopy cover was associated with a 1.4°C lower average afternoon land-surface temperature, after accounting for impervious surfaces and building density. The brief says these findings support targeted planting in the hottest neighborhoods. [S1]

For its methods, the study measured neighborhood tree canopy using 2024 aerial imagery, with canopy cover ranging from 6% to 41%. Land-surface temperature (LST) was derived from 36 cloud-free satellite passes in July of 2023, 2024 and 2025, all between 1:00 and 3:00 p.m. The researchers used a multiple regression model with average afternoon LST as the outcome and canopy cover, share of impervious surface, and building density as predictors. [S2]

The hottest neighborhood was Eastgate, with 6% canopy and an average afternoon surface temperature of 41.2°C; the coolest was Willow Park, with 41% canopy and an average of 34.8°C, a difference of 6.4°C. Share of impervious surface was the strongest single predictor of temperature, followed by canopy cover. Heat-related emergency calls during July were 23% higher in the hottest quartile of neighborhoods than in the coolest quartile. [S3]

The brief notes that LST is not the same as the air temperature people experience, that the cross-sectional design supports association rather than causation, and that the 2024 imagery may not reflect trees planted since then. Its recommendations are to prioritize planting in Eastgate and Millbrook and set a citywide target of 30% canopy cover by 2035. It estimates that planting 6,000 street trees would cost about $2.1 million over ten years. [S4]
